answerKey.primaryProblem: Tubular adenoma with focal high-grade dysplasia, completely excised, margins negative, no invasive carcinoma - a precancerous (not cancerous) finding requiring routine surveillance.
differential: Tubular adenoma with high-grade dysplasia (confirmed diagnosis)
Invasive adenocarcinoma (excluded - no invasion identified on complete sectioning)
Tubulovillous or villous adenoma (not applicable here - architecture reported as tubular)
Serrated polyp/sessile serrated lesion (not applicable - different morphology, not what was found)
keyFindings: 14 mm pedunculated sigmoid polyp removed intact in one piece
Tubular adenoma architecture with focal (not extensive) high-grade dysplasia
Dysplasia confined to the mucosa; no invasion into submucosa or deeper layers
Second pathologist concurrence on the diagnosis
plan: Explain pathology terms in plain language: adenoma = benign/precancerous polyp type; high-grade dysplasia = more abnormal-looking cells than low-grade, but still not cancer; focal = only in a small part of the polyp
Clarify that 'no invasive carcinoma' means the abnormal cells have not broken through the layer that would make this cancer
Explain negative margin means the removal appears complete at the base

State that standard guidelines support surveillance colonoscopy in 3 years for this finding, but final timing and any additional workup is determined by her gastroenterologist, factoring in her full history
Address her brother's polyp history as something to discuss further with gastroenterology/genetics if risk assessment changes
Explicitly defer scheduling, additional testing, and any treatment decisions to the gastroenterology team
Encourage her to bring written questions to her upcoming GI appointment and offer to answer any further pathology-specific questions before then
redFlags: Rectal bleeding, unintentional weight loss, or iron-deficiency anemia (not reported here; would warrant more urgent gastroenterology attention if present)
Finding of invasive carcinoma, positive margins, or lymphovascular invasion (not present in this report) would change management substantially and require earlier gastroenterology/surgical input
educationPoints: High-grade dysplasia is a description of cell appearance within a polyp, not a stage of cancer; it means the cells look more abnormal and have more potential to progress if left behind, not that cancer is already present
'Focal' means the finding was limited to part of the polyp on the slides examined, not throughout it
A negative margin and complete excision in one piece are reassuring features that reduce the chance that abnormal tissue was left behind
Surveillance intervals (e.g., 3 years) are based on established guidelines balancing the small risk of missed or recurrent polyps against the burden of repeat colonoscopy
Family history details (such as a sibling with polyps) can affect future risk assessment and screening intervals, but formal risk assessment is done by the gastroenterologist, not the pathologist
The pathologist's role is to accurately describe and diagnose the tissue; decisions about further testing, intervals, and treatment belong to the treating clinician

mismatches.patientClaim: Renee believes her brother's polyps mean colon cancer runs strongly in her family and that this should have changed how urgently her case was handled.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Documented history notes only a brother with polyps in his 40s; there is no first-degree relative with colorectal cancer on record, and her case was managed as average-risk screening based on the information available at the time.
mismatches.teachingPoint: A relative with polyps is relevant family history worth discussing further, but it is not the same as a relative with colon cancer; accurate risk stratification requires clarifying exactly what was found in the relative and should be revisited with gastroenterology, not assumed to have been missed.

patient.name: Renee Okafor
patient.appearance: A woman in her mid-40s with short natural hair, wearing a cardigan over a blouse, seated at a tidy home desk with a laptop and a notepad with handwritten questions visible. Her posture is upright and alert; she maintains steady eye contact with the camera and her expression shows controlled worry rather than panic.

persona.personality: Detail-oriented, articulate, and self-advocating; wants precise answers and is uncomfortable with vague reassurance.
persona.communicationStyle: Direct and organized, often refers to notes she has written down, asks follow-up questions if an answer feels incomplete.
persona.emotionalState: Anxious but composed; working hard to stay rational and gather information rather than panic.
persona.background: Born in the United Kingdom to Nigerian parents, moved to the United States in her twenties for work, now settled in Atlanta with her husband. Works in hospital billing, which has given her comfort reading medical documents but not necessarily understanding clinical terminology. Enjoys gardening and running a small book club on weekends.
speechExamples: Okay, so walk me through this like I'm smart but not a doctor.
I wrote down my questions so I don't forget anything.
I need to understand this before I can calm down, not the other way around.
Is there anything in here that you would consider a red flag that I'm missing?
I appreciate you not just telling me not to worry.
concerns: Whether 'high-grade dysplasia' means she already has colon cancer
Whether the polyp was completely removed and nothing was left behind
Whether her brother's polyp history means she is at higher inherited risk
Whether she should wait three weeks for her gastroenterology appointment or seek care sooner
Whether she needs additional tests like a CT scan or genetic testing now

scenario.studentBrief: You are the on-call pathology resident fielding a patient-requested telehealth consultation. Renee Okafor, 44, had her first colonoscopy after a positive stool screening test, which found a single 14 mm pedunculated polyp in the sigmoid colon, removed intact. Her pathology report shows tubular adenoma with focal high-grade dysplasia, negative margins, no invasive carcinoma. She found this report on her patient portal, researched the terms online, and believes she may have colon cancer. Her gastroenterology follow-up is three weeks away. She asked for a pathology consult to understand the report before that appointment.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Patient requests explanation of a colon polyp pathology report showing 'high-grade dysplasia,' which she fears means she has cancer.
scenario.openingLine: I got my polyp results on the online portal and it says 'high-grade dysplasia,' and when I looked that up it said cancer, so I wanted to talk to someone before my GI appointment, which isn't for three more weeks.
tasks: Explain in plain language what was examined (the polyp, how it was processed) and define each pathology term in the report: tubular adenoma, high-grade dysplasia, focal, margin status, invasive carcinoma.
Directly and clearly address whether this report means she has colon cancer, correcting her misunderstanding without dismissing her fear.
Explain what is known (complete excision, clear margin, no invasion) and what remains for gastroenterology to decide (surveillance timing, risk stratification given family history).
Explain the general rationale for a 3-year surveillance colonoscopy interval for this type of finding in a way she can bring back to her GI appointment.

Explore the family history mismatch (brother with polyps vs. her assumption about inherited cancer risk) respectfully, and hand back next-step decisions (timing of GI visit, any additional testing) to her gastroenterologist rather than deciding this yourself.

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at home at her desk in Atlanta, Georgia
profile.summary: A 44-year-old woman undergoes her first colonoscopy after a positive stool screening test, and pathology reveals a tubular adenoma with focal high-grade dysplasia, completely excised with negative margins and no invasive carcinoma. The case exercises a pathology resident's ability to translate a precancerous (not cancerous) diagnosis into clear lay language, address a patient's self-directed internet research and anxiety, and appropriately hand back surveillance timing and family-history risk stratification to the treating gastroenterologist.
profile.title: Explaining a Tubular Adenoma with High-Grade Dysplasia After First Screening Colonoscopy
